children.name: Prior Art and Clearance Searching
children.blurb: Prior art and clearance searching covers patentability, validity, freedom to operate, and trademark availability work before filing or launch.

children.name: Trademark Filing and Specimens
children.blurb: Trademark filing and specimens covers the preparation, submission, and examination of applications to register a mark, including the evidence of use in commerce that supports the filing.

children.name: Licensing Synthetic Assets and Likeness
children.blurb: This page covers how organizations license rights in AI-generated or AI-modified assets and in synthetic representations of a person's voice, face, or persona.

children.name: Patent Claim Drafting
children.blurb: Patent claim drafting is the process of writing the numbered claims that define the legal scope of protection in a patent application.

children.name: Infringement Detection and Enforcement
children.blurb: Infringement detection and enforcement covers identifying unauthorized use of protected marks, copyrighted works, patents, trade dress, and other intellectual property across digital and physical channels.

sections.body: This field covers how AI tools are used in the practical work of intellectual property law: searching for prior art before a patent filing, preparing trademark applications and specimens, drafting patent claims, licensing synthetic assets and likenesses, and detecting infringement. In current practice, AI is not replacing lawyers but doing narrow retrieval and drafting tasks. For example, clearance searching tools compare a proposed mark or invention against large databases of existing registrations and technical literature, returning ranked lists of similar entries. Trademark filing software can generate specimen mockups and check application fields for consistency. Patent claim drafting assistants propose claim language from a described invention, and infringement detection systems scan marketplaces or code repositories for likely copies. These are real, deployed functions, not speculative research.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The work is uneven. Prior art searching is the most mature, because it is fundamentally a retrieval problem with large, well structured datasets, and current tools can surface relevant references faster than manual review, though they still miss non-obvious equivalents and require human judgment. Trademark filing and specimen generation are reliable for routine, low risk applications but struggle with nuanced issues like acquired distinctiveness or ornamental refusal. Patent claim drafting remains an assistive task, not an autonomous one, because claim scope depends on legal strategy and examiner behavior that models cannot yet predict. Licensing synthetic assets and likeness is legally unsettled, and the site tracks 92 active intellectual property lawsuits, which reflects how often ownership and consent questions end up in court. Infringement detection works well for exact or near exact copying, such as image reuse or code similarity, but is weak at detecting paraphrased or transformed infringement. The honest limit is that these tools reduce search and drafting time, they do not yet make final legal determinations.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: A reader would start with Prior Art and Clearance Searching to understand how AI finds existing inventions or marks before filing, then move to Trademark Filing and Specimens for the mechanics of preparing an application. Licensing Synthetic Assets and Likeness sits apart because it deals with rights in AI generated outputs and digital personas, which connects back to clearance when those assets are used commercially. Patent Claim Drafting shows how AI assists in the most technically demanding writing task in patent prosecution, and Infringement Detection and Enforcement closes the loop by describing how AI monitors for unauthorized use after rights are granted. Together the pages move from pre-filing search, to filing, to licensing, to drafting, and finally to enforcement, which is the full lifecycle of an intellectual property practice.
